entries.title: 4624: An account was successfully logged on
entries.summary: Records every successful logon and, crucially, the LogonType that tells you whether it was someone at the keyboard, a network share, a service, or an RDP session.

entries.title: 4625: An account failed to log on
entries.summary: A logon attempt was rejected. The SubStatus code is the key field, it distinguishes a fat-fingered password from a disabled account or a locked-out user.

entries.title: 4634 / 4647: An account was logged off
entries.summary: Marks the end of a logon session. 4647 is a user-initiated logoff; 4634 is the session teardown. Pair with 4624 by LogonId to measure how long a session lasted.

entries.title: 4648: A logon was attempted using explicit credentials
entries.summary: Someone logged on with credentials different from their current session, runas, a scheduled task, or a tool connecting to a remote host with alternate creds.

entries.title: 4672: Special privileges assigned to new logon
entries.summary: Fires when a logon is granted one or more sensitive/administrative privileges. It is logged at logon time, before the account has necessarily done anything.

entries.title: 4673 / 4674: A privileged service was called
entries.summary: Records the actual use of a sensitive privilege (4673) or an operation on a privileged object (4674), as opposed to 4672 which only records assignment.

entries.title: 4720: A user account was created
entries.summary: A new local or domain user account was created. On endpoints this is rare and high-signal; on domain controllers it is routine but still worth baselining.

entries.title: 4722 / 4725 / 4726: Account enabled, disabled, or deleted
entries.summary: Lifecycle changes to an account: 4722 enabled, 4725 disabled, 4726 deleted. Re-enabling a dormant or previously disabled account is a common attacker move.

entries.title: 4728 / 4732 / 4756: Member added to a privileged group
entries.summary: An account was added to a security group. When the group is a privileged one (Administrators, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins), this is a direct privilege-escalation signal.

entries.title: 4740: A user account was locked out
entries.summary: An account crossed the failed-logon threshold and was locked. CallerComputerName points at the machine generating the failures.

entries.title: 4768: A Kerberos TGT was requested (AS-REQ)
entries.summary: A domain account requested a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket, effectively the domain logon event, recorded on the DC.

entries.title: 4769: A Kerberos service ticket was requested (TGS-REQ)
entries.summary: An account requested a service ticket for a specific SPN. This is the event that exposes Kerberoasting (T1558.003).

entries.title: 4771: Kerberos pre-authentication failed
entries.summary: The DC-side record of a failed Kerberos authentication, the domain equivalent of a 4625 for password guessing against domain accounts.

entries.title: 4776: NTLM credential validation
entries.summary: Records NTLM authentication attempts (success and failure). The go-to event for tracking legacy NTLM auth and NTLM-based brute force.

entries.title: 4688: A new process has been created
entries.summary: The single most useful execution event: what ran, from where, with what command line, and under which parent. Turn on command-line capture or you lose most of its value.

entries.title: PowerShell 4104: Script block logging
entries.summary: Logs the full text of every script block PowerShell runs, after deobfuscation. This is the highest-fidelity view of what PowerShell actually did.

entries.title: 7045: A new service was installed
entries.summary: The Service Control Manager installed a new service. This lands on both persistence (services survive reboot) and lateral movement (PsExec-style remote execution creates a temporary service).

entries.title: 4697: A service was installed in the system (Security log)
entries.summary: The Security-log counterpart to System-log 7045. Useful when you centralise on the Security channel and want service installs in the same stream as logons.

entries.title: 4698: A scheduled task was created
entries.summary: A scheduled task was registered. Tasks are a top-tier persistence and execution mechanism (T1053.005), they survive reboot and can run as SYSTEM.

entries.title: WMI-Activity 5857–5861: WMI operations and subscriptions
entries.summary: The WMI-Activity/Operational log is the main native record of WMI abuse. Event 5861 in particular captures permanent event subscriptions used for stealthy persistence.

entries.title: RDP 1149 / 21 / 25: Remote Desktop session events
entries.summary: The dedicated RDP session logs. Together with Security 4624 type 10, they reconstruct who connected over RDP, from where, and when they reconnected.

entries.title: 4778 / 4779: A session was reconnected / disconnected
entries.summary: Records reconnection (4778) and disconnection (4779) of interactive sessions, typically RDP. Disconnect-without-logoff leaves a session alive in the background.

entries.title: Run / RunOnce keys: autostart persistence
entries.summary: The most common persistence location on Windows. Anything listed here runs automatically at user logon (HKCU) or system start (HKLM). RunOnce entries run once and delete themselves.

entries.title: Winlogon Shell / Userinit: logon persistence
entries.summary: Winlogon's Shell and Userinit values control what launches when a user logs on. Appending a payload (comma-separated) is a durable, high-privilege persistence technique.

entries.title: Services registry: service persistence & hijack
entries.summary: Services are defined entirely in the registry. Attackers create new services, hijack an existing service's ImagePath/ServiceDll, or set a FailureCommand to gain SYSTEM-level, reboot-surviving persistence.

entries.title: Image File Execution Options: debugger hijack
entries.summary: IFEO lets you attach a 'debugger' that launches in place of a target executable. Attackers point accessibility binaries (sethc.exe, utilman.exe) at cmd.exe for a pre-logon SYSTEM shell, or hijack other binaries for persistence.

entries.title: WMI event subscription persistence
entries.summary: A fileless persistence technique: a WMI filter (trigger) is bound to a consumer (action) so attacker code runs on an event, with nothing in the usual Run/Startup locations.

entries.title: Persistence locations: where to look
entries.summary: Persistence is not one answer, it is a set of autostart extensibility points (ASEPs). Junior analysts should learn the whole checklist rather than a single key.

entries.title: 1102: The audit log was cleared
entries.summary: The Security event log was cleared. Because Windows always logs this action (even as the log is wiped), 1102 is a near-guaranteed anti-forensics indicator.

entries.title: 104: An event log was cleared (non-Security logs)
entries.summary: The 104 counterpart to 1102 for logs other than Security. Attackers clear System, PowerShell, and Sysmon logs to erase execution and service-install evidence.

entries.title: 4719: System audit policy was changed
entries.summary: The audit policy was modified. Attackers disable specific auditing subcategories to go dark before acting, and the disable itself is logged here.

entries.title: 4657: A registry value was modified
entries.summary: A native way to watch specific registry keys change without Sysmon. Because it needs a SACL and is noisy, you enable it only on high-value keys.

entries.title: Defender 5001 / 5007 / 1116 / 1117: Microsoft Defender events
entries.summary: The Defender operational events that reveal both real detections (1116/1117) and tampering (5001 disable, 5007 config/exclusion changes).

entries.title: Sysmon 1: Process creation
entries.summary: Sysmon's process-creation event, the richest native execution telemetry available, with hashes, full parent/child command lines, and the binary's original filename.

entries.title: Sysmon 3: Network connection
entries.summary: Maps processes to their network connections. The key event for tying an outbound C2 connection back to the exact process that made it.

entries.title: Sysmon 10: Process access (LSASS)
entries.summary: Records one process opening a handle to another. Scoped to LSASS, it is the premier detection for credential dumping (T1003.001).

entries.title: Sysmon 11 / 12 / 13 / 14: File and registry events
entries.summary: Sysmon's file- and registry-monitoring family. Event 13 (registry value set) is the low-friction way to watch autostart keys and catch persistence as it is written.

entries.title: Sysmon 22: DNS query
entries.summary: Attributes DNS lookups to the process that made them, filling the gap where network logs show the resolver but not the originating process.

entries.title: Sysmon 19 / 20 / 21: WMI event monitoring
entries.summary: Sysmon's dedicated WMI-persistence events. Together, 19/20/21 capture the trigger, action, and binding of a permanent WMI event subscription as they are created.

entries.title: Prefetch: evidence of execution
entries.summary: Prefetch files prove a program executed, how many times, and when, even if the binary is now deleted. A cornerstone 'evidence of execution' artifact.

entries.title: Amcache.hve: execution & presence with hashes
entries.summary: A registry hive tracking application presence and execution, and, unusually for a Windows artifact, the SHA1 of many recorded binaries.

entries.title: Shimcache (AppCompatCache): execution/presence order
entries.summary: The Application Compatibility Cache tracks executables the OS evaluated for shimming. A classic 'was this binary here' artifact, valuable because it survives deletion.

entries.title: SRUM: application & network resource usage
entries.summary: The System Resource Usage Monitor database records per-application network and resource usage over roughly 30–60 days, a rare native source of historical bytes-sent data.

entries.title: LNK files & Jump Lists: file/opened-item history
entries.summary: LNK shortcuts and Jump Lists record which files a user opened, when, and from where, including files on USB drives and network shares that are no longer connected.

entries.title: UserAssist / BAM: GUI & background program execution
entries.summary: Two per-user execution artifacts: UserAssist tracks GUI-launched programs with run counts, and BAM/DAM records the last execution time of executables per user.

entries.title: ShellBags: folder browsing history
entries.summary: ShellBags record folders a user browsed in Explorer, including deleted, removable, and network locations, proving a user navigated to a path even after it is gone.

entries.title: Scheduled task files: on-disk task definitions
entries.summary: The forensic, on-disk view of scheduled tasks. Pairing the Tasks XML files with the TaskCache registry catches tasks hidden from the normal UI.

entries.title: Startup folders: drop-a-file persistence
entries.summary: The simplest persistence: drop a file or shortcut into a Startup folder and it launches at logon, no registry edit or admin rights required for the per-user folder.

entries.title: 4767: A user account was unlocked
entries.summary: An account that was locked out (see 4740) has been unlocked. Pairs with lockout events to show the response side of a brute-force incident.

entries.title: 1100: The event logging service was shut down
entries.summary: The Windows Event Log service stopped. Expected during a clean shutdown, but a 1100 with no corresponding reboot can mean an attacker stopped logging to go dark.

entries.title: LSASS credential dumping: detection
entries.summary: Reading LSASS memory to extract credentials (T1003.001). Detect it via the process handle opened on lsass.exe, any dump file written, and the tell-tale command lines.

entries.title: T1110: Brute Force
entries.summary: Systematically guessing credentials. On Windows this is the story told by failed-logon telemetry, the shape of the failures tells you which sub-technique you are looking at.

entries.title: T1110.001: Password Guessing
entries.summary: Guessing passwords for a specific known account against a live service, the noisiest brute-force variant, frequently triggering lockouts.

entries.title: T1110.003: Password Spraying
entries.summary: Trying one or a few common passwords against many accounts to stay under lockout thresholds. Quieter than guessing and easy to miss without cross-account aggregation.

entries.title: T1110.004: Credential Stuffing
entries.summary: Replaying username/password pairs stolen from other breaches. Because the credentials are often correct, it can produce immediate successes with little failed-logon noise.

entries.title: T1078: Valid Accounts
entries.summary: Using legitimate credentials to blend in across initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, and evasion. The successful logons look normal, detection is about deviation from baseline.

entries.title: T1059: Command and Scripting Interpreter
entries.summary: Abusing built-in command and script interpreters to run code. The parent umbrella for PowerShell, cmd, and WSH execution on Windows.

entries.title: T1059.001: PowerShell
entries.summary: Using PowerShell for download cradles, in-memory execution, and post-exploitation. The single most abused interpreter on Windows.

entries.title: T1027: Obfuscated Files or Information
entries.summary: Hiding payloads and commands through encoding, packing, or obfuscation to defeat static detection.

entries.title: T1053.005: Scheduled Task
entries.summary: Using Task Scheduler for persistence and execution, including SYSTEM-level and remotely-created tasks.

entries.title: T1547.001: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
entries.summary: The most common autostart persistence: registry Run keys and Startup-folder items that launch at logon or boot.

entries.title: T1543.003: Windows Service
entries.summary: Installing or hijacking a Windows service for SYSTEM-level, reboot-surviving persistence (and often execution).

entries.title: T1569.002: Service Execution
entries.summary: Executing commands by installing and starting a (usually transient) Windows service, the mechanism behind PsExec and many C2 lateral-movement modules.

entries.title: T1021.001: Remote Desktop Protocol
entries.summary: Moving laterally via interactive RDP sessions using valid credentials.

entries.title: T1021.002: SMB / Windows Admin Shares
entries.summary: Using SMB and the hidden administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$, IPC$) to move laterally and stage tools.

entries.title: T1546.003: WMI Event Subscription
entries.summary: Fileless persistence via permanent WMI event subscriptions that run attacker code on a trigger.

entries.title: T1546.008: Accessibility Features
entries.summary: Abusing accessibility binaries to get a pre-authentication SYSTEM shell from the logon screen.

entries.title: T1047: Windows Management Instrumentation
entries.summary: Using WMI for execution, reconnaissance, and lateral movement, a native, low-footprint technique.

entries.title: T1112: Modify Registry
entries.summary: Creating, modifying, or deleting registry data for persistence, evasion, or to store configuration.

entries.title: T1070.001: Clear Windows Event Logs
entries.summary: Clearing Windows event logs to remove evidence, a deliberate anti-forensics act that is itself logged.

entries.title: T1562.001: Disable or Modify Tools
entries.summary: Disabling or weakening security tooling, turning off Defender, adding exclusions, or killing agents, to clear the way for tools.

entries.title: T1562.002: Disable Windows Event Logging
entries.summary: Turning off Windows auditing so subsequent actions go unlogged, often paired with, or preceding, log clearing.

entries.title: T1558.003: Kerberoasting
entries.summary: Requesting RC4 service tickets for SPNs in bulk to crack service-account passwords offline.

entries.title: T1003: OS Credential Dumping
entries.summary: Harvesting account credentials from LSASS, the SAM, NTDS.dit, or via DCSync, the gateway to escalation and lateral movement.

entries.title: T1071: Application Layer Protocol (C2)
entries.summary: Blending command-and-control traffic into common application protocols (HTTP/S, DNS) to evade network defences.

entries.title: T1071.004: DNS (C2)
entries.summary: Tunnelling command-and-control or data over DNS queries and responses.

entries.title: T1098: Account Manipulation
entries.summary: Modifying accounts, group membership, state, credentials, to maintain or escalate access.

entries.title: T1136: Create Account
entries.summary: Creating new local or domain accounts for persistent access, frequently followed by adding them to privileged groups.

entries.title: PowerShell 4103: Module / pipeline logging
entries.summary: Module logging records pipeline execution details (cmdlets and parameters). It complements 4104 script-block logging with per-invocation context.

entries.title: Sysmon 8: CreateRemoteThread
entries.summary: Records cross-process thread creation, the core primitive of code injection (T1055). Attackers inject into trusted processes to hide and to steal tokens.

entries.title: Sysmon 7: Image (DLL) loaded
entries.summary: Records DLLs and modules loaded by processes. Scoped well, it catches DLL search-order hijacking and side-loading (T1574.002).

entries.title: Sysmon 15: File create stream hash (ADS / Mark-of-the-Web)
entries.summary: Captures files created with NTFS alternate data streams, including the Zone.Identifier stream that marks internet-downloaded files (Mark-of-the-Web).

entries.title: Sysmon 17 / 18: Named pipe created / connected
entries.summary: Records named-pipe creation and connection. Named pipes are used for local inter-process C2 (SMB beacons) and privilege-escalation via impersonation.

entries.title: 5140 / 5145: A network share object was accessed
entries.summary: Records access to SMB shares. Paired with network logons (4624 type 3), it exposes lateral movement over admin shares and tool staging.

entries.title: 4662: An operation was performed on a directory object (DCSync)
entries.summary: Records directory-object access on domain controllers. Filtered to the replication rights, it is the detection for DCSync, pulling password hashes by impersonating a DC.

entries.title: AppInit_DLLs: inject-into-every-process persistence
entries.summary: A legacy mechanism that loads listed DLLs into nearly every GUI process. Rarely used legitimately today, so a populated value is high-signal.

entries.title: COM hijacking: CLSID persistence
entries.summary: Hijacks a COM object's registration so attacker code loads whenever a legitimate application instantiates that object, stealthy, often user-level persistence.

entries.title: LSA Security Packages / SSP: credential-theft persistence
entries.summary: A malicious Security Support Provider registered here is loaded into LSASS and can log every plaintext credential at authentication time, persistence plus credential theft.

entries.title: BITS jobs: download & persistence via Background Intelligent Transfer
entries.summary: BITS is a trusted Windows transfer service. Attackers use it to download payloads quietly and to persist via jobs that run a command on completion.

entries.title: $MFT / $UsnJrnl: filesystem timeline
entries.summary: The NTFS Master File Table and USN change journal are the backbone of filesystem forensics, timelining file creation, modification, renaming, and deletion.

entries.title: T1055: Process Injection
entries.summary: Running code inside another (usually trusted) process to evade defences, escalate, and access another process's memory.

entries.title: T1574: Hijack Execution Flow (DLL)
entries.summary: Placing a malicious library where a trusted program will load it (via search order, side-loading, or path interception) so attacker code runs with the host's trust.

entries.title: T1564: Hide Artifacts
entries.summary: Concealing files, data, and execution from users and defenders via alternate data streams, hidden attributes, or removing the Mark-of-the-Web.

entries.title: T1197: BITS Jobs
entries.summary: Abusing the Background Intelligent Transfer Service to download payloads stealthily and to persist via completion-command jobs.

entries.title: T1558.001 / .002: Golden & Silver Tickets
entries.summary: Forging Kerberos tickets from stolen key material: a Golden Ticket (krbtgt hash) grants domain-wide access; a Silver Ticket (service hash) grants access to one service.

entries.summary: Splunk SPL searches indexed events, extracts and normalises fields, aggregates behaviour and enriches entities so an analyst can move from raw data to a testable detection or scoped investigation.

entries.title: YARA rules

entries.title: journalctl and Linux logging

entries.title: Packet capture and Wireshark

entries.title: PsTools for defensive administration
